title: Decorators & Closures: The Python Function-Wrapping Handbook
summary: A dense field guide to how Python functions capture state and get wrapped — from first-class functions and closure cells through decorator syntax, functools.wraps, argument forwarding, parameterized and class-based decorators, stacking order, and the real-world patterns (caching, retry, timing, auth) plus the bugs everyone hits.

chapters.title: Functions Are Objects
points: Functions are first-class objects: can be assigned to variables, stored in lists/dicts, passed as args, returned from other functions
`def greet(): ...` binds a function object to the name `greet`; `greet` is the object, `greet()` is the call
Example: `f = greet; f()` calls the same underlying function — the name is just a reference
Function attributes you can inspect: `__name__`, `__doc__`, `__module__`, `__qualname__`, `__defaults__`, `__dict__`
You can attach arbitrary attributes: `greet.calls = 0` works because functions have a `__dict__`
Higher-order function = takes a function as arg and/or returns a function; `map`, `filter`, `sorted(key=...)` are builtin examples
`lambda x: x*2` is an anonymous function object — same type (`types.FunctionType`) as a `def`, just no statement body
Callable ≠ function: any object with `__call__` is callable; `callable(obj)` tests it
Why it matters: decorators are only possible because functions can be passed in and returned out
Gotcha: `f = greet()` stores the *return value*, not the function — the most common beginner slip

chapters.title: Nested Functions & Scope (LEGB)
points: A function defined inside another function is created fresh on every call of the outer function
LEGB lookup order: Local → Enclosing → Global → Built-in
Local: names assigned inside the current function. Enclosing: names in an outer *function* (not module) scope
Assignment inside a function makes the name local for the whole function body — even before the assignment line
`UnboundLocalError: local variable 'x' referenced before assignment` — caused by assigning to a name you also read from an outer scope
`global x` rebinds a module-level name; `nonlocal x` rebinds the nearest enclosing *function* name
`nonlocal` requires the name to already exist in an enclosing scope, else `SyntaxError: no binding for nonlocal 'x' found`
Counter example: `def outer(): n=0; def inner(): nonlocal n; n+=1; return n; return inner`
Mutating without rebinding needs no keyword: `lst.append(1)` works on an enclosing list; `lst = [1]` does not
Scope is determined at compile time from the syntax, not at runtime by what values exist

chapters.title: Closures: What They Are & How They Work
points: Closure = a nested function plus the captured bindings from its enclosing scope, kept alive after the outer function returns
Three conditions: nested function, references a name from the enclosing scope, outer function returns the inner one
Canonical example: `def make_adder(n): def add(x): return x + n; return add` → `add5 = make_adder(5); add5(3) == 8`
Inspect it: `add5.__closure__` returns a tuple of `cell` objects; `add5.__closure__[0].cell_contents` is `5`
`add5.__code__.co_freevars` lists the captured names (`('n',)`); the outer function's `co_cellvars` lists what it exports
Closures capture *variables by reference (cells)*, not values at definition time — the cell is shared, not copied
The classic bug: `[lambda: i for i in range(3)]` all return `2`; fix with a default arg `lambda i=i: i` or a factory function
Each call to the outer function creates independent cells — two `make_adder` results never share state
Closures keep enclosing objects alive (they hold references), which can hold memory longer than expected
Closure vs class: a closure with one method ≈ an object with one attribute; classes win when you need multiple methods or introspection

chapters.title: Decorator Syntax: @ Is Just Sugar
points: `@deco` above `def f(): ...` is exactly `f = deco(f)` executed right after the `def`
A decorator is any callable taking one argument (the function) and returning a replacement
Minimal decorator: `def deco(fn): def wrapper(*a, **kw): return fn(*a, **kw); return wrapper`
The decorator body runs once at *import/definition* time; the wrapper body runs on every call
The wrapper must `return fn(...)` — forgetting the `return` silently makes every call yield `None`
The original function survives only as the closed-over `fn`; the module name now points at the wrapper
Decorators work on any def: module functions, nested functions, methods, and classes
`@` accepts any expression that evaluates to a callable (since PEP 614): `@registry[name]`, `@obj.method`, `@make_deco(x)`
Side-effect-only decorator: register the function in a dict and `return fn` unchanged — no wrapper needed
Applying a decorator to an already-imported function (monkeypatching) works: `mod.f = deco(mod.f)`

chapters.title: Preserving Metadata with functools.wraps
points: Naive wrappers destroy identity: `f.__name__` becomes `'wrapper'`, `f.__doc__` becomes the wrapper's docstring or `None`
Fix: `@functools.wraps(fn)` on the wrapper — copies metadata from the wrapped function onto the wrapper
`wraps` copies `__module__`, `__name__`, `__qualname__`, `__doc__`, `__dict__` (updated, not replaced), and sets `__wrapped__ = fn`
`wraps` is a thin wrapper over `functools.update_wrapper(wrapper, fn)`; the tuples `WRAPPER_ASSIGNMENTS` / `WRAPPER_UPDATES` are configurable
`__wrapped__` lets `inspect.signature(f)` report the *original* signature; pass `follow_wrapped=False` to see the wrapper's
`inspect.unwrap(f)` follows the `__wrapped__` chain back to the undecorated function
Without `wraps`, `help(f)`, `pydoc`, Sphinx autodoc, pytest test names, and debugger tracebacks all show the wrong name
`wraps` copies references only — it does NOT copy the signature into the wrapper's own `__code__`; `*args, **kwargs` is still what actually binds
Failure mode: `functools.wraps` on a wrapper for a builtin or C function can raise `AttributeError` on missing `__name__`/`__qualname__`
Rule of thumb: every decorator that returns a new function gets `@wraps`, no exceptions

chapters.title: Passing Arguments Through the Wrapper
points: Universal forwarding signature: `def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): return fn(*args, **kwargs)` — accepts and relays anything
`*args` collects positional args into a tuple; `**kwargs` collects keyword args into a dict
At the call site `fn(*args, **kwargs)` is *unpacking*, the mirror of collecting — same syntax, opposite direction
Inspecting a specific parameter safely: `bound = inspect.signature(fn).bind(*args, **kwargs); bound.apply_defaults(); bound.arguments['user']`
Never index `args[0]` blindly — the caller may have passed it as a keyword, and for methods `args[0]` is `self`
Modifying args before the call: rebuild the tuple (`args = (args[0].strip(),) + args[1:]`) since tuples are immutable
Modifying the result after the call: `result = fn(*a, **kw); return transform(result)`
Wrapping generators/async functions needs matching wrappers: `async def wrapper(...): return await fn(...)`, and `yield from fn(...)` for generators
Use `functools.partial` when you want to pre-bind arguments rather than wrap behavior
Gotcha: a wrapper with a *narrower* signature (`def wrapper(x)`) breaks every caller that passes extra or keyword args

chapters.title: Decorators That Take Arguments
points: `@repeat(3)` means `f = repeat(3)(f)` — `repeat(3)` is called first and must *return a decorator*
Three nested levels: factory(args) → decorator(fn) → wrapper(*a, **kw)
Full example: `def repeat(n): def deco(fn): @wraps(fn) def w(*a,**kw): for _ in range(n): r = fn(*a,**kw); return r; return w; return deco`
The factory's arguments are captured by closure and are visible in every wrapper call
Bug: writing `@repeat` instead of `@repeat(3)` passes the *function* as `n` — the error surfaces far from the cause
Optional-args pattern: support both `@deco` and `@deco(x=1)` by checking `if fn is None: return partial(deco, x=x)`
Alternative: make the first parameter keyword-only and positional-function-only — `def deco(fn=None, *, x=1)`
Factory-level validation belongs at factory time (raise on bad `n` immediately), not on first call
The factory runs once per decorated function; the decorator object it returns is not reusable state — don't cache mutable defaults there
Real-world shapes: `@lru_cache(maxsize=128)`, `@app.route('/path')`, `@pytest.mark.parametrize(...)`, `@retry(times=3, delay=1)`

chapters.title: Class-Based Decorators & Decorating Classes
points: A class is a valid decorator if instances are callable: `__init__(self, fn)` stores it, `__call__(self, *a, **kw)` runs it
Class-based decorators make per-function state explicit: `self.count += 1` beats `nonlocal count`
Use `functools.update_wrapper(self, fn)` inside `__init__` — `@wraps` decorates functions, not instances
Descriptor problem: a class-decorated *method* loses binding; the instance is not passed as `self` unless you implement `__get__`
Fix: `def __get__(self, obj, objtype): return functools.partial(self.__call__, obj)`, or just use a function-based decorator for methods
Decorating a class: `@deco class C: ...` means `C = deco(C)`; the decorator can mutate, subclass, or replace the class
Stdlib class decorators: `@dataclass`, `@functools.total_ordering`, `@typing.runtime_checkable`
Built-in method decorators: `@staticmethod` (no implicit first arg), `@classmethod` (`cls` first), `@property` (attribute-style access)
Ordering with methods: `@classmethod` must be the outermost decorator — it returns a descriptor, not a plain function
`@functools.cached_property` computes once per instance and stores the value in `__dict__`; requires the class to have a `__dict__` (no `__slots__`)

chapters.title: Stacking Order & Execution Flow
points: Stacked decorators apply bottom-up: `@a` over `@b` over `def f` becomes `f = a(b(f))`
But they *execute* top-down at call time: `a`'s wrapper runs first, then `b`'s, then the real `f`
Mnemonic: closest to `def` wraps first (innermost); highest in the file runs first (outermost)
Order matters when effects interact: `@cache` above `@log` caches log-free repeats; `@log` above `@cache` logs every call including hits
`@app.route` must be outermost — registration must see the fully decorated function
`@staticmethod`/`@classmethod` outermost; `@property` outermost over its getter
Timing decorators placed outside a retry decorator measure total elapsed time including retries; inside, per-attempt time
Debugging a stack: print `f.__wrapped__.__wrapped__` or walk with `inspect.unwrap` to confirm the chain
Each layer costs one extra Python frame per call — deep stacks show up in profiles and in tracebacks
Decorator-application side effects all fire at import time in bottom-up order, before any call happens

chapters.title: Common Uses in Practice
points: Memoization: `@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=None)` / `@functools.cache` — args must be hashable; exposes `.cache_info()` and `.cache_clear()`
Timing: record `time.perf_counter()` around the call, log the delta; use `perf_counter`, never `time.time()`, for durations
Logging/tracing: log name, args, result, and exceptions — the single most common hand-rolled decorator
Retry with backoff: loop `attempts`, catch a specific exception tuple, `time.sleep(delay * 2**i)`, re-raise on the last try
Auth/permission gates: check the current user, raise `PermissionError` or return 403 before delegating
Validation/type coercion: inspect the signature, check types against annotations, raise `TypeError` early
Rate limiting / debouncing: closure holds the last-call timestamp or a token bucket
Registration: `@register('csv')` appends the function to a plugin dict and returns it unchanged
`@contextlib.contextmanager` turns a generator into a `with`-block context manager
`@functools.singledispatch` dispatches on the first argument's type; register overloads with `@fn.register`
Framework examples worth naming: Flask `@app.route`, pytest `@fixture`, Django `@login_required`, Click `@click.command`

chapters.title: Comparisons & Trade-offs
points: Decorator vs manual wrapper call: `@` is declarative and visible at the definition; manual `f = deco(f)` is explicit and works on imported objects
Closure decorator vs class decorator: closures are terser and pickle-friendlier; classes give named state, methods, and easy inspection
Decorator vs mixin/subclass: decorators compose horizontally across unrelated functions; inheritance ties behavior to a type hierarchy
Decorator vs context manager: decorator wraps a whole *function*; `with` wraps an arbitrary *block* — `ContextDecorator` gives you both
Decorator vs middleware: middleware sits once in a request pipeline; decorators are per-handler and more granular
Cost: one extra frame + `*args/**kwargs` packing per call — negligible for I/O work, measurable in tight numeric loops
`lru_cache` trade-off: O(1) hit lookup for unbounded memory growth with `maxsize=None`; keys hold strong references to arguments
Debuggability cost: tracebacks gain wrapper frames and step-through gets noisier — `wraps` mitigates but does not remove this
Typing cost: a `*args, **kwargs` wrapper erases the signature for type checkers unless you use `ParamSpec`/`Concatenate` (PEP 612)
Readability rule: prefer a decorator when the concern is cross-cutting and repeated; prefer an explicit call when it happens once

chapters.title: Common Mistakes & Debugging
points: Forgetting `@wraps` — silent until docs, logs, or pytest report `wrapper` everywhere
Forgetting to `return` inside the wrapper, or forgetting to `return wrapper` from the decorator (decorated function becomes `None`)
Writing `@deco()` when the decorator takes no args, or `@deco` when it requires them — errors like `TypeError: deco() missing 1 required positional argument`
Late-binding capture in loops: closures see the *final* value of the loop variable; bind with a default arg or a factory
Mutable state shared across decorated functions when it lives in the factory scope instead of the decorator scope
`@lru_cache` on methods keeps `self` alive in the cache key forever — a real memory leak; prefer `cached_property` or a per-instance cache
`@lru_cache` on a function with unhashable args raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'`
Decorating with a stateful object and reusing that object across functions — state bleeds between them
Losing exception context: catching and re-raising without `raise ... from e` hides the original cause
Wrapping an `async def` with a sync wrapper returns a coroutine object that never gets awaited — `RuntimeWarning: coroutine was never awaited`
Debug toolkit: `inspect.unwrap`, `f.__wrapped__`, `f.__closure__[i].cell_contents`, `f.__code__.co_freevars`, `inspect.signature(f)`

chapters.title: Summary & Quick Reference
points: Closure = inner function + captured cells; survives the outer call and captures by reference, not by value
Decorator = callable taking a function and returning a replacement; `@d` is exactly `f = d(f)`
Template to memorize: `def deco(fn): @wraps(fn) def wrapper(*a, **kw): ...; return fn(*a, **kw); return wrapper`
Argument-taking template: factory → decorator → wrapper, three levels, closure carries the config down
Always `@functools.wraps(fn)`; always forward `*args, **kwargs`; always `return` the call's result
Stacking: bottom decorator wraps first, top decorator runs first
Introspection cheat sheet: `__name__`, `__doc__`, `__wrapped__`, `__closure__`, `__code__.co_freevars`, `inspect.signature`, `inspect.unwrap`
Stdlib worth knowing by heart: `wraps`, `update_wrapper`, `partial`, `cache` / `lru_cache`, `cached_property`, `singledispatch`, `total_ordering`, `contextmanager`
Reach for a class-based decorator when you need named per-function state; add `__get__` if it decorates methods
Use `ParamSpec` in typed codebases so decorated functions keep their signatures
Final rule: decorators are for cross-cutting concerns — logging, caching, retry, auth, timing, registration. Business logic stays in the function.
